read.sections.0.heading.source: A vote, a transition and restored independence

read.sections.0.text.note: The sentence on violence is kept as plain as the English. "Indonesia menguasainya" (Indonesia controlled it) follows the English exactly; reviewers in Indonesia should check it reads as factual, not as blame.
read.sections.0.text.back: Timor-Leste, which is also called East Timor, lies on the island of Timor. Portugal controlled it for a long time. From the 1970s, Indonesia controlled it. On 30 August 1999, East Timorese voters took part in a vote organised by the United Nations. Most chose to begin steps towards independence. After the vote, there was violence, and many people had to leave their homes. Then came a time of transition. A UN team ran the country, working together with East Timorese leaders. On 20 May 2002, Timor-Leste's independence was restored. That country first declared independence in 1975. A country can celebrate something in one day, but making schools work well for every child needs much more time.
read.sections.0.text.source: Timor-Leste, also called East Timor, is on the island of Timor. Portugal ruled it for a long time. From the 1970s, Indonesia controlled it. On 30 August 1999, East Timorese voters took part in a vote run by the United Nations. Most voted to begin a move towards independence. After the vote there was violence, and many people had to leave their homes. A transition followed. A United Nations team ran the country, working with East Timorese leaders. On 20 May 2002, Timor-Leste's independence was restored. It had first declared independence in 1975. A country can celebrate on one day, but making schools work for every child takes much longer.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: Timor-Leste is also called East Timor. Portugal controlled it for a long time. Later, Indonesia controlled it. In 1999, people there voted. Most chose to go towards independence. After that there was violence. Many people had to leave home. Then came a time of transition. A UN team helped run that country. On 20 May 2002, independence was restored. A country can celebrate in one day. But good schools for every child need much more time.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: Timor-Leste is also called East Timor. Portugal ruled it for a long time. Later, Indonesia controlled it. In 1999, people there voted. Most chose to move towards independence. After the vote there was violence. Many people had to leave their homes. Then came a transition. A United Nations team helped run the country. On 20 May 2002, independence was restored. A country can celebrate in one day. But good schools for every child take much longer.

read.sections.1.text.note: "Communities" here is "masyarakat" (local people), not "komunitas", as it means the people around each school.
read.sections.1.text.back: Rebuilding schools began in the time of transition, not after it. In March 2000, a UN report said that most children who used to go to primary school were back in class. Many schools had been repaired, often with new roofs. In some places, teachers, parents and communities helped reopen their schools. There was not yet one curriculum the same for all schools. Teachers taught in Tetum, Indonesian, Portuguese or English. In 2004, a researcher named Susan Nicolai wrote a study for UNESCO. She found that rebuilding mostly focused on buildings, and less on plans for teachers, books and language. Her study looks back at events that had passed. That study is not a diary written by a child in 1999.
read.sections.1.text.source: Rebuilding schools began during the transition, not after it. In March 2000, a United Nations report said most children who had been in primary school were back in class. Many schools had been repaired, often with new roofs. In some places, teachers, parents and communities helped restart their schools. There was no standard curriculum yet. Teachers taught in Tetum, Indonesian, Portuguese or English. In 2004, a researcher called Susan Nicolai wrote a study for UNESCO. She found that rebuilding focused mostly on buildings, and less on plans for teachers, books and language. Her study looks back at events. It is not a diary written by a child in 1999.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: Repairs to schools began in the time of transition. Those repairs did not wait until 2002. In March 2000, a UN report said most children were back in class. Many schools got new roofs. Teachers, parents and local people helped. There was not yet a curriculum for all schools. Teachers used four different languages. In 2004, Susan Nicolai wrote a study about this time. She found that people repaired buildings first. Plans for teachers, books and languages came more slowly.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Work on schools started during the transition. It did not wait until 2002. In March 2000, a UN report said most children were back in class. Many schools got new roofs. Teachers, parents and communities helped. There was no curriculum for all schools yet. Teachers used four different languages. In 2004, Susan Nicolai wrote a study about this time. She found that people fixed buildings first. Plans for teachers, books and languages came more slowly.

read.sections.2.text.note: "Many languages" is listed as UNICEF's wording for a planning challenge, not a problem in children; the teachers' note says so.
read.sections.2.text.back: The Government of Timor-Leste sets Tetum and Portuguese as the official languages. People also speak many other local languages. UNICEF, the UN agency for children, says that the country has rebuilt its schools since 2002, and now more children go to school. UNICEF also names its problems: old buildings, the many languages, and fewer school facilities in rural areas. UNICEF works together with the government to repair schools, improve the way of teaching, and build schools where pupils and parents take part. That photo shows one school in 2024. That photo cannot tell us whether the pupils there have books or trained teachers. That photo cannot show whether they have access to lessons in a language they understand.

watch.summary.back: This UNICEF report was made in 2011. This report visits a primary school in Laclubar, a town in the mountains of Timor-Leste. After the 1999 vote, many people left their homes. That school was left without a roof, tables or chairs. When people came back, the local school leaders asked the teachers to come back. Parents gave chairs, tables and other things the school needed. The minister of education says that the country had to start its schools again from the beginning. The government worked together with UNICEF to plan new lessons, repair schools and train teachers. Now that school uses a child-friendly way of teaching. Pupils and parents take part in school life.
watch.summary.source: This UNICEF report was made in 2011. It visits a primary school in Laclubar, a town in the mountains of Timor-Leste. After the vote in 1999, many people left their homes. The school was left with no roof, desks or chairs. When people came back, local school leaders asked teachers to return. Parents gave chairs, tables and other things the school needed. The minister of education says the country had to start its schools again from the beginning. The government worked with UNICEF to plan new lessons, fix schools and train teachers. Now the school uses a child-friendly way of teaching. Students and parents take part in school life.

educatorNotes.0.back: Aim: learners choose two priorities for rebuilding education, give a source-based reason for each, and name one trade-off. Step for reading evidence: ask what a school needs besides walls. A good answer gives two priorities supported by the UN report, the IIEP study or UNICEF, and a reasonable trade-off. Misunderstandings to straighten out: "independence immediately solved the problem of education", "education work only began after 2002", and "all learners speak both official languages".

educatorNotes.1.note: "Consultation" is "jajak pendapat", the usual Indonesian name for the 1999 vote. "23 March" is kept in English as it appears on the page.
educatorNotes.1.back: Languages: the Government of Timor-Leste sets Portuguese and Tetum (Tétum, the national language) as official languages, English and Indonesian as working languages, and about 15 other local languages. Talk about this without framing it as a lack: many languages are a strength and a planning question, not a problem in children. Notes on the sources: UNICEF's page gives percentages with no date, so this lesson does not use them as current figures. The IIEP summary dates the popular consultation to September 1999 (the vote was on 30 August; its result came out in September). That UN news item only shows "23 March"; its address and content (UNTAET, the earlier international force) place it in 2000.
